fuentes/saga-de-erik-el-rojo/soporte.texto: Two manuscripts: the Hauksbók (around 1302–1310) and the Skálholtsbók (15th century)

fuentes/saga-de-erik-el-rojo/resumen.texto: Anonymous Icelandic saga that narrates the colonization of Greenland by Erik the Red and the voyages to Vinland, above all the attempted colony of Thorfinn Karlsefni and Gudrid. It recounts the trade of red cloth for furs with the natives, whom it calls skrælingar, the capture at Markland of two native children, whom the Norsemen took away and baptized, and the fights that led them to abandon the site. It attributes to Leif Erikson the accidental discovery of Vinland and the conversion of Greenland.

fuentes/saga-de-erik-el-rojo/por_que_imp.texto: Together with the Saga of the Greenlanders, it is the only written account of the Norse voyages to America. The archaeology of L’Anse aux Meadows confirmed that the Norse reached America, although the saga was written more than two centuries later and mixes family tradition, legendary elements and a religious purpose: to exalt the conversion to Christianity.

fuentes/saga-de-los-groenlandeses/resume.texto: Short saga that recounts six voyages west from Greenland: the sighting of land by Bjarni Herjólfsson, the exploration by Leif Erikson, the expedition of his brother Thorvald, the settlement of Karlsefni and the voyage of Freydís. It tells that Thorvald’s men killed eight natives who were sleeping under their leather boats, that Thorvald died in the attack that followed, and that Freydís had her Icelandic partners killed.

fuentes/saga-de-los-groenlandeses/por_qu.texto: It is generally considered somewhat older and less elaborate than the Saga of Erik the Red, and it is the main source on Leif’s role. It shows the violence between Norsemen and natives, and among the Norsemen themselves, as it was remembered in Iceland two centuries later.

fuentes/libro-de-los-asentamientos/autor.texto: Anonymous (versions by Sturla Þórðarson and Haukr Erlendsson)

fuentes/libro-de-los-asentamientos/sopor.texto: Versions from the 13th and 14th centuries (Sturlubók, Hauksbók) based on a lost 12th-century original

fuentes/libro-de-los-asentamientos/resum.texto: Register of some four hundred settlers of Iceland, their lands, families and lawsuits. It includes the story of Erik the Red: the killings that led to his banishment, the exploration of Greenland and the fleet of settlers of which, according to the text, fourteen of twenty-five ships arrived.

fuentes/libro-de-los-asentamientos/por_q.texto: It is the most detailed source on the origins of the Greenland colony, although the surviving versions are about three centuries later than the events and were reworked by their copyists.

fuentes/espejo-del-rey/resumen.texto: Norwegian didactic dialogue between a father and his son on commerce, the court and the wonders of the world. It devotes several chapters to Greenland: the ice, the auroras, the bears and walruses, livestock raising, what the Greenlanders imported (iron and wood) and what they sold (furs, walrus-hide ropes and tusks).

fuentes/espejo-del-rey/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most complete description of Norse Greenland written while the colony existed, and it confirms the importance of walrus ivory in its economy.

fuentes/espejo-del-rey/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by Laurence M. Larson (1917) on Internet Archive

fuentes/anales-islandeses/soporte.texto: Several series of annals in Icelandic manuscripts

fuentes/anales-islandeses/resumen.texto: Annual chronicles written in Icelandic monasteries and houses. They record news from Greenland: the submission to the king of Norway (1261), the voyages of the bishops, an attack by skrælingar in 1379 that killed eighteen Greenlanders and carried off two boys as slaves, and the burning for witchcraft of a man in Greenland in 1407.

fuentes/anales-islandeses/por_que_import.texto: They are the few records dated year by year of Norse Greenland in its final centuries, though terse and written far from the island.

fuentes/descripcion-de-groenlandia-barda.texto: Old Norse (preserved in Danish and Norwegian translations)

Description of the fjords, churches and farms of Norse Greenland attributed to Ívar Bárðarson, administrator of the see of Garðar. It tells that he went with others to the Western Settlement to drive out the skrælingar and found it empty, with sheep, goats and cattle loose but no people.
It is the only written testimony on the abandonment of the Western Settlement. The original was lost and the text survives in copies from the 16th century, so its exact wording is uncertain.

fuentes/a-true-discourse-best/titulo.texto: A True Discourse of the Late Voyages of Discoverie, for the Finding of a Passage to Cathaya by the North-West

fuentes/a-true-discourse-best/resumen.texto: Account of the three voyages of Martin Frobisher written by one of his officers. It describes the Inuit of Baffin Island, their clothing, their kayaks, their weapons and their dwellings, the disappearance of five sailors in 1576, the capture of one man that year and of a man, a woman and a child in 1577, and the 1577 combat in which several Inuit died.

fuentes/a-true-discourse-best/por_que_im.texto: It is the first extensive English description of the Inuit, and it documents the capture of people to take them to England. The Inuit oral traditions that Charles Francis Hall collected in 1861 still remembered those visits.

fuentes/det-gamle-gronlands-nye-perlustr.texto: Description of Greenland written by Hans Egede after fifteen years on the island: the climate, the animals, seal and whale hunting, dwellings, customs, language and beliefs of the Greenlanders, and their angakkut, whom he presents as deceivers. It includes engravings and was translated into German, into English (1745) and into other languages.
For a century it was the main European source on the Inuit of Greenland, and it shows, through a missionary’s eyes, the first years of Danish colonization.
English translation of 1745 on Internet Archive

fuentes/grammatica-groenlandica/resumen.texto: First grammar of Greenlandic, written to train missionaries. It completes the Greenlandic, Danish and Latin dictionary that Poul Egede had published in 1750.

fuentes/grammatica-groenlandica/por_que_.texto: Together with the dictionary, it is the written basis for the study of Greenlandic and part of Denmark’s missionary project, which evangelized in the language of the Inuit.

fuentes/historie-von-gronland/resumen.texto: History of Greenland written by a Moravian brother after visiting the Neu-Herrnhut mission in 1761–1762. It describes the nature and life of the Greenlanders and narrates the Lutheran and Moravian missions, including the smallpox epidemic of 1733–1734.

fuentes/historie-von-gronland/por_que_im.texto: It is the most complete source on 18th-century Greenland after Egede, and it was translated into English in 1767; it reflects the viewpoint of the Moravian mission, rival of the Lutheran one.

fuentes/historie-von-gronland/leer.0.tit.texto: English translation of 1767 on Internet Archive

fuentes/grammatik-kleinschmidt/resumen.texto: Greenlandic grammar that established regular orthography for the language. Together with the dictionary that Kleinschmidt published in 1871, it served as the basis for writing Greenlandic until the reform of 1973.

fuentes/grammatik-kleinschmidt/por_que_i.texto: It is an example of missionary work on an Indigenous American language that ended up giving its speakers a written language of their own, later used in the press and the school.

fuentes/journey-hearne/titulo.texto: A Journey from Prince of Wales’s Fort in Hudson’s Bay to the Northern Ocean

fuentes/journey-hearne/resumen.texto: Account of the journeys of Samuel Hearne between 1769 and 1772, with Chipewyan guides, to the Coppermine River and the Arctic Ocean. It describes the life of the Dene and the massacre of an Inuit camp at Bloody Falls in July 1771 by the men of his guide Matonabbee.

fuentes/journey-hearne/por_que_importa.texto: It is the only written source on the Bloody Falls massacre and a document of the wars between Dene and Inuit. It was published three years after Hearne’s death with additions by the editor, so some details are debated.

fuentes/journey-hearne/leer.0.titulo.texto: Edition by Joseph B. Tyrrell on Project Gutenberg

fuentes/tales-and-traditions-of-the-eski.texto: Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo

Selection of oral stories from Greenland that Rink gathered from the 1850s with Inuit narrators and writers, with a study of their society, beliefs and laws. It includes accounts of encounters, trade and fights with the Norsemen, such as that of the chief Ungortoq.
It is the main early collection of Inuit oral tradition and the source of what Greenlanders themselves remembered of the Norsemen, a memory transmitted for centuries that must be read as such.

fuentes/origen-de-los-indios-garcia/titu.texto: Origin of the Indians of the New World and the West Indies

fuentes/origen-de-los-indios-garcia/resu.texto: Treatise by the Dominican Gregorio García, who had lived in Peru, on how the Indians came to America. It sets out and discusses the theories of his time: crossing by land or sea from Asia, the ten lost tribes of Israel, the Carthaginians, Plato’s Atlantis and others, and concludes that the Indians descend from several peoples.

fuentes/origen-de-los-indios-garcia/por_.texto: It shows how the origin of the Americans was debated in the 16th and 17th centuries, with the Bible and classical authors as evidence. Several of these theories later returned as myths without basis.

fuentes/early-man-in-south-america/sopor.texto: Bulletin 52 of the Bureau of American Ethnology (Smithsonian Institution)

fuentes/early-man-in-south-america/resum.texto: Report written by Hrdlička with William H. Holmes, Bailey Willis, Fred E. Wright and Clarence N. Fenner after reviewing in 1910, in Argentina, the remains and sites that Florentino Ameghino attributed to the Tertiary. It concludes that none proves a great antiquity of humans and that the human remains are those of recent Indigenous people.

fuentes/early-man-in-south-america/por_q.texto: It dismantled Ameghino’s theory of the American origin of humanity. His rejection of any glacial antiquity proved in turn mistaken, as Folsom showed in 1927.

fuentes/alliance-and-conflict-burch/titu.texto: Alliance and Conflict: The World System of the Iñupiat Eskimos

fuentes/alliance-and-conflict-burch/resu.texto: Study of the relations among the Iñupiat nations of northwest Alaska in the early 19th century, reconstructed from oral tradition and written sources. It describes their alliances, trade fairs and wars, with surprise raids, massacres of entire villages and armor of bone and ivory.

fuentes/alliance-and-conflict-burch/por_.texto: It shows, through oral tradition and documents, that war among Arctic peoples was frequent before Europeans settled in the region, against the image of the Eskimos as peaceful peoples.

fuentes/colapso-diamond/titulo.texto: Collapse: How Societies Choose to Fail or Succeed

fuentes/colapso-diamond/resumen.texto: Comparative essay on the collapse of societies. Its chapters on Greenland attribute the end of the Norse to environmental degradation, cooling, attachment to a European livestock economy, the conservatism of the Church and contempt for the Inuit, from whom they supposedly did not learn to hunt or fish. Another chapter attributes the fall of Rapa Nui to deforestation caused by its own inhabitants, an “ecocide.”

fuentes/colapso-diamond/por_que_importa.texto: It spread a very influential explanation. Specialists object that isotopes show a diet increasingly based on seals, that the colony lived from the walrus ivory trade and that its end may have been a gradual emigration. For Rapa Nui, Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo (The Statues That Walked, 2011) object that Polynesian rats played a role in the deforestation and that the population collapsed from diseases and later slave raids after the European contact of 1722.

fuentes/bonnichsen-v-estados-unidos/auto.texto: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit

fuentes/bonnichsen-v-estados-unidos/resu.texto: Ruling that upheld the 2002 district court decision: since no link had been shown between the Kennewick Man and any present-day Indigenous people, his remains were not “Native American” within the meaning of the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), and the plaintiff scientists could study them.

fuentes/bonnichsen-v-estados-unidos/por_.texto: It was the central ruling in the dispute between scientists and Indigenous peoples over ancient human remains. The 2015 genome later showed the kinship that the court had considered unproven, and the remains were returned to the tribes.

fuentes/monte-verde-dillehay/titulo.texto: Monte Verde: A Late Pleistocene Settlement in Chile

fuentes/monte-verde-dillehay/resumen.texto: Monograph on the excavations of Monte Verde II, a camp preserved under peat: remains of a row of wood-framed houses, hearths, stone, bone and wood tools, edible and medicinal plants, seaweed and bones of gomphotheres (a relative of the mastodon), dated to about 12,500 radiocarbon years (about 14,500 calibrated).

fuentes/monte-verde-dillehay/por_que_imp.texto: It was the evidence that weighed most in accepting that there were people at the southern tip of America before Clovis.

fuentes/meltzer-1997-monte-verde/titulo.texto: On the Pleistocene Age of Monte Verde, Southern Chile

fuentes/meltzer-1997-monte-verde/resumen.texto: Report by the archaeologists who in January 1997 reviewed the site and its collections, among them skeptics of Clovis such as C. Vance Haynes. They concluded that the site was human and was about 12,500 radiocarbon years old.

fuentes/meltzer-1997-monte-verde/por_que.texto: It marked the end of the “Clovis first” consensus. Stuart Fiedel (1999) and later Haynes himself raised doubts about the documentation of the pieces, which Dillehay answered.

fuentes/haynes-1964/titulo.texto: Fluted Points: Their Age and Dispersion

fuentes/haynes-1964/resumen.texto: He gathered the radiocarbon dates from sites with fluted points and proposed that Clovis hunters entered through the ice-free corridor and spread rapidly across the continent.

fuentes/haynes-1964/por_que_importa.texto: It is the basis of the “Clovis first” model, dominant until 1997.

fuentes/waters-stafford-2007/autor.texto: Michael R. Waters and Thomas W. Stafford

fuentes/waters-stafford-2007/resumen.texto: Radiocarbon redating of the Clovis sites: the complex would have lasted about two centuries, between about 11,050 and 10,800 radiocarbon years. Such a short span makes it hard for its bearers to have been the first to populate the whole continent.

fuentes/waters-stafford-2007/por_que_imp.texto: It reinforced the idea that there were populations before Clovis.

fuentes/waters-2020-edad-de-clovis/titul.texto: The Age of Clovis: From 13,050 to 12,750 Calibrated Years

fuentes/waters-2020-edad-de-clovis/resum.texto: New review of the dates from Clovis sites that places the complex between 13,050 and 12,750 calibrated years before the present, about three centuries.

fuentes/waters-2020-edad-de-clovis/por_q.texto: It is the Clovis chronology most used today.

fuentes/martin-1973/resumen.texto: Model according to which a small band of hunters entered southern Canada about 11,500 years ago, grew rapidly and advanced in a front that killed off the megafauna before it learned to fear humans, reaching the south of the continent in about a thousand years.

fuentes/martin-1973/por_que_importa.texto: It is the classic formulation of the “overkill” or “blitzkrieg” hypothesis.

fuentes/grayson-meltzer-2003/autor.texto: Donald K. Grayson and David J. Meltzer

fuentes/grayson-meltzer-2003/resumen.texto: They review the sites with evidence of megafauna hunting: in North America only about fourteen show hunting of mammoth or mastodon, and none of the other thirty-odd extinct genera. They conclude that overkill is not demonstrated and give more weight to climate change.

fuentes/grayson-meltzer-2003/por_que_imp.texto: It is the most cited critique of Martin’s hypothesis, which still has defenders.

fuentes/greenberg-1987/resumen.texto: Classifies the Indigenous languages of the Americas, by “mass lexical comparison” of word lists, into three groups: Eskimo-Aleut, Na-Dene and Amerind, the last including all the others. Greenberg, Christy Turner and Stephen Zegura linked these groups to three migrations from Asia.

fuentes/greenberg-1987/por_que_importa.texto: It was widely disseminated beyond linguistics. Specialists rejected Amerind as a demonstrated family, although genetics later confirmed some later migration in the north.

fuentes/campbell-1988/resumen.texto: Detailed critique of Amerind: errors in the data, words badly segmented or attributed to the wrong languages, resemblances explainable by chance or borrowing, and lack of regular phonetic correspondences. It proposes keeping the families demonstrated by the comparative method.

fuentes/campbell-1988/por_que_importa.texto: It expresses the position of most specialists in the languages of the Americas.

fuentes/stanford-bradley-2012/titulo.texto: Across Atlantic Ice: The Origin of America’s Clovis Culture

fuentes/stanford-bradley-2012/resumen.texto: Book by Dennis Stanford and Bruce Bradley proposing that the ancestors of Clovis were people of the Solutrean culture of France and the Iberian Peninsula who crossed the North Atlantic following the edge of the ice during the last glaciation. It relies on similarities in knapping technique and on finds from the east coast of the United States.

fuentes/stanford-bradley-2012/por_que_im.texto: It is the most complete formulation of the Solutrean hypothesis, rejected by most archaeologists and contradicted by ancient genomes.

fuentes/straus-meltzer-goebel-2005/titul.texto: An Ice Age Atlantis? The “Connection” Between Solutrean and Clovis

fuentes/straus-meltzer-goebel-2005/autor.texto: Lawrence G. Straus, David J. Meltzer and Ted Goebel

fuentes/straus-meltzer-goebel-2005/resum.texto: Critiques of the Solutrean hypothesis: the Solutrean ended about five thousand years before Clovis, there is no evidence of navigation or of hunting on sea ice, Solutrean points were not fluted, and the technical resemblances are explained by convergence.

fuentes/straus-meltzer-goebel-2005/por_q.texto: It summarizes the archaeological arguments against the hypothesis; the Anzick-1 genome (2014) added the genetic one.

fuentes/guidon-delibrias-1986/titulo.texto: Carbon-14 Dates Indicate Human Presence in America 32,000 Years Ago

fuentes/guidon-delibrias-1986/resumen.texto: Niède Guidon and Georgette Delibrias published radiocarbon dates of charcoal from supposed hearths at Pedra Furada of up to about 32,000 years, associated with quartz and quartzite stones that they interpreted as tools.

fuentes/guidon-delibrias-1986/por_que_im.texto: It opened the debate on a very ancient human presence in South America.

fuentes/meltzer-adovasio-dillehay-1994/t.texto: On a Pleistocene Human Occupation at Pedra Furada, Brazil

fuentes/meltzer-adovasio-dillehay-1994/r.texto: After visiting the site, the authors argue that the “tools” in the oldest layers may be stones broken by falling from the top of the cliff and that the charcoal may come from natural fires. They ask for clearer evidence before accepting a Pleistocene occupation.

fuentes/meltzer-adovasio-dillehay-1994/p.texto: It is the main critique of Pedra Furada; Guidon and her team rejected it.

fuentes/raghavan-2014-malta/titulo.texto: The Genome of an Upper Paleolithic Siberian Reveals the Dual Ancestry of Native Americans

fuentes/raghavan-2014-malta/resumen.texto: Genome of a child buried at Mal’ta, near Lake Baikal, about 24,000 years ago. It shows that between 14 and 38 percent of Native American ancestry comes from a Siberian population related to Western Europeans, and the rest from a population of East Asia.

fuentes/raghavan-2014-malta/por_que_impo.texto: It explained “non-Asian” traits of some ancient American skulls without the need for migrations from Europe.

fuentes/rasmussen-2014-anzick/titulo.texto: The Genome of a Late Pleistocene Human from a Clovis Burial in Western Montana

fuentes/rasmussen-2014-anzick/resumen.texto: Genome of Anzick-1, a child buried with Clovis tools about 12,600 years ago. He is a direct ancestor or close relative of the ancestors of many present-day Indigenous people, closer to those of Central and South America than to those of the north.

fuentes/rasmussen-2014-anzick/por_que_im.texto: It proved that the Clovis people belonged to the same population as Native Americans and contradicted the Solutrean hypothesis.

fuentes/rasmussen-2015-kennewick/titulo.texto: The Ancestry and Affiliations of Kennewick Man

fuentes/rasmussen-2015-kennewick/resumen.texto: Genome of Kennewick Man, about 8,500 years old. It relates him closely to present-day Native Americans, and among those studied, above all to the Colville Confederated Tribes, which had claimed his remains.

fuentes/rasmussen-2015-kennewick/por_que.texto: It refuted the interpretation of his skull as “Caucasoid” or Polynesian and was decisive for the return of the remains.

fuentes/raghavan-2015/titulo.texto: Genomic Evidence for the Pleistocene and Recent Population History of Native Americans

fuentes/raghavan-2015/resumen.texto: With ancient and present-day genomes, it proposes that the ancestors of Native Americans separated from East Asians no more than 23,000 years ago, entered America in a single migration and split about 13,000 years ago into a northern and a southern branch.

fuentes/raghavan-2015/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the two studies from 2015 that established the current genetic model; it discusses the Australasian signal that Skoglund found.

fuentes/skoglund-2015/titulo.texto: Genetic Evidence for Two Founding Populations of the Americas

fuentes/skoglund-2015/resumen.texto: It finds in Amazonian peoples such as the Suruí and the Karitiana a small genetic component related to populations of Australia, New Guinea and the Andaman Islands, which does not appear in other Indigenous peoples. It attributes it to an unknown source population, the “Population Y.”

fuentes/skoglund-2015/por_que_importa.texto: It reopened the question of whether there was more than one founding population in South America.

fuentes/moreno-mayar-2018/titulo.texto: The Genome of a Terminal Pleistocene Alaskan Child Reveals the First Founding Population of Native Americans

fuentes/moreno-mayar-2018/resumen.texto: Genome of a baby from Upward Sun River (Alaska) about 11,500 years old. It defines the “Ancient Beringians,” separated from the other Native Americans about 20,000 years ago, and holds that the founding population separated from East Asians about 25,000 years ago.

fuentes/moreno-mayar-2018/por_que_import.texto: It supports the model of a long pause in Beringia before entry into the continent.

fuentes/moreno-mayar-2018-dispersiones/t.texto: The First Human Dispersals Within the Americas

fuentes/moreno-mayar-2018-dispersiones/r.texto: With fifteen ancient genomes from Alaska to Patagonia, six of them more than 10,000 years old, it shows that all of them, including those of skulls considered “Paleoamerican” such as those of Lagoa Santa, are related to present-day Native Americans, and that the first settlers dispersed rapidly southward in several migrations. It finds traces of the Australasian signal in an individual from Lagoa Santa about 10,400 years old.

fuentes/moreno-mayar-2018-dispersiones/p.texto: Together with the study by Posth and others from the same year, it contradicted the idea of a distinct “Paleoamerican” population, and it left open the question of the Australasian signal.

fuentes/posth-2018/titulo.texto: Reconstructing the Deep Population History of Central and South America

fuentes/posth-2018/resumen.texto: It studies 49 ancient genomes from Central and South America, up to about 11,000 years old. It finds that the first South Americans, including those of Lagoa Santa, descend from the same population as the other Indigenous peoples, with a Clovis-related contribution that was later replaced.

fuentes/posth-2018/por_que_importa.texto: It did not find the Australasian signal in the ancient genomes it studied and contradicted the idea of a distinct “Paleoamerican” population.

fuentes/bennett-2021/titulo.texto: Evidence of Humans in North America During the Last Glacial Maximum

fuentes/bennett-2021/resumen.texto: It presents human footprints in sediments of an ancient lake in White Sands (New Mexico), dated by seeds of an aquatic plant to about 23,000 to 21,000 calibrated years.

fuentes/bennett-2021/por_que_importa.texto: If the dates are correct, there were people south of the ice during the glaciation, thousands of years earlier than accepted.

fuentes/pigati-2023/titulo.texto: Independent Age Estimates Resolve the Controversy over Ancient Human Footprints at White Sands

fuentes/pigati-2023/resumen.texto: It answers the objection that aquatic seeds could give dates that are too old: it dates conifer pollen and quartz grains from the same layers and obtains matching ages of about 23,000 to 21,000 years.

fuentes/pigati-2023/por_que_importa.texto: It convinced many of the skeptics, although some still doubt the association between the footprints and the dated layers.

fuentes/gilbert-2008/titulo.texto: DNA from Pre-Clovis Human Coprolites in Oregon

fuentes/gilbert-2008/autor.texto: M. Thomas P. Gilbert et al.

fuentes/gilbert-2008/resumen.texto: It identifies mitochondrial DNA of Native American lineages in coprolites from Paisley Caves dated to about 14,300 calibrated years, more than a millennium before Clovis.

fuentes/gilbert-2008/por_que_importa.texto: It was one of the first genetic proofs of human presence before Clovis; the possible contamination was debated.

fuentes/tamm-2007/titulo.texto: The Beringian Standstill and the Spread of Native American Founders

fuentes/tamm-2007/resumen.texto: With mitochondrial DNA lineages, it proposes that the ancestors of Native Americans were isolated in Beringia for thousands of years, where they differentiated from Asians, before expanding rapidly across the Americas.

fuentes/tamm-2007/por_que_importa.texto: It formulated the hypothesis of the “Beringian standstill,” which later genomes broadly supported.

fuentes/pedersen-2016/titulo.texto: Postglacial Viability and Colonization of North America’s Ice-Free Corridor

fuentes/pedersen-2016/resumen.texto: With environmental DNA and pollen from lake sediments, it shows that the corridor between the ice sheets of western Canada did not have enough plants and animals to sustain hunters until about 12,600 years ago.

fuentes/pedersen-2016/por_que_importa.texto: It implies that the first settlers, who came before that date, could not have entered through the corridor, and it reinforces the Pacific coastal route.

fuentes/holen-2017/titulo.texto: A 130,000-Year-Old Archaeological Site in Southern California

fuentes/holen-2017/resumen.texto: It interprets broken mastodon bones and stones found beside them in San Diego, dated by uranium series to about 130,000 years, as the work of hominins who broke the bones.

fuentes/holen-2017/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most extreme claim of human antiquity in America; most archaeologists reject it because the fractures may have natural causes.

fuentes/ardelean-2020/titulo.texto: Evidence for Human Occupation in Mexico Around the Last Glacial Maximum

fuentes/ardelean-2020/resumen.texto: It presents nearly two thousand chipped stones from the Chiquihuite Cave (Zacatecas) in layers dated to about 30,000 years ago.

fuentes/ardelean-2020/por_que_importa.texto: If the stones were tools, human presence in America would be much older; several specialists hold that they are stones broken by natural causes.

fuentes/piperno-2009/titulo.texto: Maize Starch Grains and Phytoliths from the Early Ninth Millennium BP in the Balsas Valley

fuentes/piperno-2009/resumen.texto: It finds maize starch and phytoliths on grinding tools from the Xihuatoxtla rock shelter (Guerrero), in layers about 8,700 calibrated years old, in the same region where the teosinte from which it descends grows.

fuentes/piperno-2009/por_que_importa.texto: It is the oldest archaeological evidence of maize.

fuentes/piperno-flannery-2001/titulo.texto: The Earliest Archaeological Maize from the Highlands of Mexico

fuentes/piperno-flannery-2001/resumen.texto: Dolores Piperno and Kent Flannery directly date three cobs from Guilá Naquitz Cave (Oaxaca) to about 6,250 calibrated years, already showing traits of a domesticated plant.

fuentes/piperno-flannery-2001/por_que_im.texto: They are the oldest maize cobs dated directly.

fuentes/matsuoka-2002/titulo.texto: A Single Domestication of Maize, Demonstrated by Microsatellite Genotyping

fuentes/matsuoka-2002/resumen.texto: It compares hundreds of maize and teosinte plants from across the Americas and concludes that maize arose from a single domestication of teosinte from the Balsas Valley, about 9,000 years ago, and spread from there.

fuentes/matsuoka-2002/por_que_importa.texto: It is the genetic basis of the origin of maize that the archaeology of Xihuatoxtla later confirmed.

fuentes/spooner-2005/titulo.texto: A Single Domestication of the Potato

fuentes/spooner-2005/resumen.texto: With genetic markers of cultivated and wild potatoes, it concludes that the potato was domesticated only once, in southern Peru, north of Lake Titicaca, from wild species of the Solanum brevicaule complex.

fuentes/spooner-2005/por_que_importa.texto: It replaced the idea of several independent domestications along the Andes.

fuentes/smith-1997-cucurbita/titulo.texto: Early Domestication of Cucurbita pepo in the Americas 10,000 Years Ago

fuentes/smith-1997-cucurbita/resumen.texto: It directly dates squash seeds and rinds from Guilá Naquitz Cave and shows domestication traits from about 10,000 to 8,000 years ago.

fuentes/smith-1997-cucurbita/por_que_imp.texto: It showed that plants were domesticated in Mesoamerica thousands of years before maize.

fuentes/olsen-schaal-1999/titulo.texto: Evidence on the Origin of Manioc

fuentes/olsen-schaal-1999/autor.texto: Kenneth M. Olsen and Barbara A. Schaal

fuentes/olsen-schaal-1999/resumen.texto: It compares cultivated manioc with wild populations of its species and concludes that it was domesticated on the southern edge of the Amazon basin, in present-day Brazil, and not in Mesoamerica.

fuentes/olsen-schaal-1999/por_que_import.texto: It located the origin of one of the crops that feed hundreds of millions of people today.

fuentes/kaplan-lynch-1999/titulo.texto: Phaseolus in Archaeology: AMS Dates and Their Significance for Pre-Columbian Agriculture

fuentes/kaplan-lynch-1999/autor.texto: Lawrence Kaplan and Thomas F. Lynch

fuentes/kaplan-lynch-1999/resumen.texto: It directly radiocarbon dates by accelerator mass spectrometry beans from sites in Mexico and Peru. Those from Guitarrero Cave, previously attributed to about 10,000 years, turn out to be about 4,300 radiocarbon years old.

fuentes/kaplan-lynch-1999/por_que_import.texto: It corrected one of the most cited dates for early American agriculture.

fuentes/bruno-whitehead-2003/titulo.texto: Chenopodium Cultivation and Formative Period Agriculture at Chiripa, Bolivia

fuentes/bruno-whitehead-2003/autor.texto: Maria C. Bruno and William T. Whitehead

fuentes/bruno-whitehead-2003/resumen.texto: It studies quinoa seeds from Chiripa, beside Lake Titicaca, and shows that from the Early Formative period, around 1500 BC, domesticated forms were cultivated.

fuentes/bruno-whitehead-2003/por_que_imp.texto: It is one of the best-dated archaeological proofs of quinoa domestication.

fuentes/kadwell-2001/titulo.texto: Genetic Analysis Reveals the Wild Ancestors of the Llama and the Alpaca

fuentes/kadwell-2001/soporte.texto: Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 268, 2575–2584

fuentes/kadwell-2001/resumen.texto: With mitochondrial DNA and microsatellites, it shows that the llama descends from the guanaco and the alpaca from the vicuña, with much later hybridization between the two.

fuentes/kadwell-2001/por_que_importa.texto: It resolved the origin of the two largest domesticated animals of the Americas.

fuentes/speller-2010/titulo.texto: Ancient Mitochondrial DNA Reveals the Complexity of Turkey Domestication by Indigenous North Americans

fuentes/speller-2010/resumen.texto: With DNA from turkey remains from sites in the southwestern United States, it shows that a distinct lineage was domesticated or raised there, different from the Mesoamerican domestic turkey, which was raised mainly for its feathers.

fuentes/speller-2010/por_que_importa.texto: It showed that the turkey was domesticated at least twice in the Americas.

fuentes/thornton-2012/titulo.texto: The Oldest Mexican Turkeys in the Maya Region

fuentes/thornton-2012/resumen.texto: It identifies at El Mirador (Guatemala) remains of turkeys of the species from central Mexico, outside their natural range, dated between about 300 BC and AD 100.

fuentes/thornton-2012/por_que_importa.texto: It is the oldest evidence of the Mesoamerican domestic turkey and of its long-distance trade.

fuentes/firestone-2007/titulo.texto: Evidence for an Extraterrestrial Impact 12,900 Years Ago

fuentes/firestone-2007/resumen.texto: It proposes that the impact or airburst of a comet about 12,900 years ago caused fires, the cooling of the Younger Dryas, the extinction of megafauna and the end of Clovis, based on microspherules, nanodiamonds and other evidence in a layer found at many sites.

fuentes/firestone-2007/por_que_importa.texto: It launched the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis, rejected by most specialists.

fuentes/holliday-2023/titulo.texto: Full Refutation of the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis

fuentes/holliday-2023/resumen.texto: It reviews fifteen years of studies and concludes that the indicators of the supposed impact were not replicated, do not have the date attributed to them, or have terrestrial explanations.

fuentes/holliday-2023/por_que_importa.texto: It summarizes the majority position against the hypothesis, which its defenders still maintain.

fuentes/ioannidis-2020/titulo.texto: Indigenous American Gene Flow into Polynesia Before the Settlement of Easter Island

fuentes/ioannidis-2020/resumen.texto: With genomes of Polynesians and present-day Indigenous Americans, it finds in several islands of Eastern Polynesia a small Indigenous American ancestry related to the Zenú of Colombia, incorporated around 1150–1230 AD.

fuentes/ioannidis-2020/por_que_importa.texto: It is the genetic evidence of contact between America and Polynesia before Columbus, which the spread of the sweet potato already suggested.

fuentes/rasmussen-2010-saqqaq/titulo.texto: Ancient Human Genome Sequence of an Extinct Paleo-Eskimo

fuentes/rasmussen-2010-saqqaq/resumen.texto: The first complete genome of an ancient human, obtained from a lock of hair about 4,000 years old from the Saqqaq culture, in western Greenland. Its closest relatives are peoples of the northeastern tip of Siberia, not the present-day Inuit or other Indigenous Americans.

fuentes/rasmussen-2010-saqqaq/por_que_im.texto: It showed that the Paleo-Eskimos arrived in a migration of their own from Siberia, distinct from that of the Inuit.

fuentes/raghavan-2014-artico/titulo.texto: The Genetic Prehistory of the New World Arctic

fuentes/raghavan-2014-artico/resumen.texto: With ancient genomes from across the American Arctic, it concludes that the Paleo-Eskimos, from Saqqaq to Dorset, were a single population that lived in isolation for about 4,000 years and disappeared around 1300–1500 with little mixing with the Thule, ancestors of the Inuit.

fuentes/raghavan-2014-artico/por_que_imp.texto: It resolved the relationship between the two great populations of the American Arctic.

fuentes/friesen-arnold-2008/titulo.texto: The Date of the Thule Migration

fuentes/friesen-arnold-2008/autor.texto: T. Max Friesen and Charles D. Arnold

fuentes/friesen-arnold-2008/resumen.texto: With new dates from sites in the western Canadian Arctic, it argues that the eastward migration of the Thule from Alaska did not begin before the 13th century and was very rapid.

fuentes/friesen-arnold-2008/por_que_impo.texto: It shortened the chronology of Inuit expansion and brought it closer in time to the Norse presence in Greenland.

fuentes/jenness-1925/titulo.texto: A New Eskimo Culture in Hudson Bay

fuentes/jenness-1925/resumen.texto: Based on pieces from Cape Dorset (Baffin Island) and other sites, it distinguishes an Arctic culture earlier than the Inuit, with its own tools and art, which he calls Dorset.

fuentes/jenness-1925/por_que_importa.texto: It was the first to identify the Dorset culture.

fuentes/mathiassen-1927/soporte.texto: Report of the Fifth Thule Expedition (1921–1924), vol. IV

fuentes/mathiassen-1927/resumen.texto: Report on the excavations of the Fifth Thule Expedition in the central Canadian Arctic, mainly at Naujan. It defines the Thule culture, of whale hunters with semi-subterranean houses of stone and whalebone, as the ancestor of the Inuit.

fuentes/mathiassen-1927/por_que_importa.texto: It is the founding text of Thule archaeology.

fuentes/ingstad-1977/titulo.texto: The Discovery of a Norse Settlement in America

fuentes/ingstad-1977/resumen.texto: Report on the excavations at L’Anse aux Meadows: plans of the eight buildings, Norse objects (a bronze pin, a spindle whorl, iron nails and slag) and radiocarbon dates from around the year 1000.

fuentes/ingstad-1977/por_que_importa.texto: It is the archaeological proof of Norse presence in America.

fuentes/kuitems-2021/titulo.texto: Evidence for European Presence in the Americas in AD 1021

fuentes/kuitems-2021/resumen.texto: Using the mark left in tree rings by a cosmic radiation spike in 993, it dates three pieces of wood cut with metal tools at L’Anse aux Meadows: the trees were felled in 1021.

fuentes/kuitems-2021/por_que_importa.texto: It gives the first exact year of European presence in America, 471 years before Columbus’s first voyage.

fuentes/star-2018/titulo.texto: Ancient DNA Reveals the Chronology of the Walrus Ivory Trade from Norse Greenland

fuentes/star-2018/soporte.texto: Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 285, 20180978

fuentes/star-2018/resumen.texto: With DNA from walrus ivory pieces found in Europe, it shows that from the 12th century most of it came from walruses of western Greenland, hunted by the Norse.

fuentes/star-2018/por_que_importa.texto: It confirmed that walrus ivory was the economic mainstay of the colony and its link with Europe.

fuentes/arneborg-2012/titulo.texto: The Food Economy of Norse Greenland, from around 980 to around 1450

fuentes/arneborg-2012/soporte.texto: Journal of the North Atlantic, special volume 3

fuentes/arneborg-2012/resumen.texto: With isotopes from the bones of Norse people buried in Greenland, it shows that their diet shifted from relying mainly on livestock to relying largely on seals and other marine animals, which became most of what they ate.

fuentes/arneborg-2012/por_que_importa.texto: It contradicts the idea that the Norse failed to adapt to Arctic resources.

personas/erik-el-rojo/resumen.texto: Norwegian raised in Iceland, where his father had fled for homicides, and who was banished from there for other homicides. According to the Book of the Icelanders and the Book of Settlements, he explored Greenland during his banishment and around 985 brought settlers: of twenty-five ships, fourteen arrived. He founded the farm of Brattahlid and gave the island the name “Green Land” to attract settlers.

personas/leif-erikson/resumen.texto: Son of Erik the Red. According to the Saga of the Greenlanders he sailed west around the year 1000 and named Helluland, Markland and Vinland; the Saga of Erik the Red says he arrived by accident and credits him with the Christianization of Greenland at the request of King Olaf Tryggvason. The two sagas were written about two centuries later and differ in details.

personas/thorfinn-karlsefni/resumen.texto: Icelandic merchant who, according to the two Vinland sagas, tried to establish a colony there around 1010 with men, women and livestock. He traded with the natives, whom the Norse called skrælingar, fought with them and abandoned the site after three winters, according to the Saga of Erik the Red.

personas/gudrid-thorbjarnardottir/resume.texto: Icelander who, according to the sagas, lived in Greenland and traveled to Vinland with her husband Thorfinn Karlsefni; there her son Snorri, the first child of European parents born in America of whom there is a written record, would have been born. The Saga of the Greenlanders says that in old age she made a pilgrimage to Rome and ended her life as a nun in Iceland.

personas/freydis-eiriksdottir/resumen.texto: Daughter of Erik the Red. The Saga of the Greenlanders says that she led a voyage to Vinland with two Icelandic brothers, had them and their men killed to keep their ship, and killed the five women of the group with an axe; the Saga of Erik the Red shows her, by contrast, driving off the skrælingar. They are accounts written two centuries later, with no other confirmation.

personas/ivar-bardarson/resumen.texto: Norwegian cleric sent to Greenland by the bishop of Bergen around 1341, who administered the see of Garðar for about twenty years. A description of Greenland attributed to him, preserved only in later copies, tells that he went to the Western Settlement and found it without people, with cattle loose, and attributed this to the skrælingar.

personas/hans-egede/resumen.texto: Norwegian Lutheran pastor who arrived in Greenland in 1721, with support from the crowns of Denmark and Norway and from Bergen merchants, to look for the descendants of the Norse colonists and convert them to Lutheranism: he found only Inuit. He founded the mission and the post that in 1728 became Godthåb (Nuuk), learned Greenlandic and wrote the first modern description of the island. His campaign against the angakkut (shamans) and Inuit beliefs is the most debated part of his mission.

personas/poul-egede/resumen.texto: Son of Hans Egede: he arrived in Greenland as a child, learned Greenlandic from the Inuit and was a missionary there. Back in Copenhagen he published the first dictionary (1750) and the first grammar (1760) of Greenlandic, and a translation of the New Testament.

personas/samuel-kleinschmidt/resumen.texto: Son of Moravian missionaries, born in Greenland. His grammar of 1851 and his dictionary of 1871 fixed the orthography of Greenlandic used until 1973; he also translated the Bible and wrote school books.

personas/hinrich-rink/resumen.texto: Danish geologist of German origin, inspector of South Greenland between 1857 and 1868. He created local councils with Greenlandic representatives, promoted the printing press and the newspaper Atuagagdliutit (1861), and collected hundreds of Inuit oral tales, which he published in Danish and in English.

personas/aron-de-kangeq/resumen.texto: Greenlandic hunter and artist who, encouraged by Rink, illustrated Inuit legends in engravings and watercolors, among them tales of struggles between Inuit and Norse. His images were printed in Godthåb and are among the first works of an Inuit artist known by name.

personas/knud-rasmussen/resumen.texto: Explorer and ethnographer born in Greenland, to a Danish father and a partly Inuit mother. He led the Fifth Thule Expedition (1921–1924), which crossed the Arctic by sledge from Greenland to Alaska, collected oral traditions and showed the unity of the Inuit languages from one end to the other.

personas/therkel-mathiassen/resumen.texto: Danish archaeologist of the Fifth Thule Expedition. In 1927, based on his excavations at Naujan and other sites in the central Canadian Arctic, he defined the Thule culture, that of the ancestors of the Inuit.

personas/diamond-jenness/resumen.texto: New Zealand anthropologist who worked in Canada. In 1925, studying pieces from Cape Dorset (Baffin Island) and other sites, he identified an Arctic culture earlier than the Inuit, which he called Dorset.

personas/martin-frobisher/resumen.texto: English seaman who made three voyages to Baffin Island (1576–1578) in search of the Northwest Passage and gold. He captured Inuit and took them to England, where they soon died, and in 1577 his men killed several Inuit in a fight, according to George Best’s account. The tons of ore he took to England contained no gold.

personas/helge-ingstad/resumen.texto: Norwegian explorer and writer who, following the sagas and old maps and with the help of a local resident, George Decker, identified the Norse site of L’Anse aux Meadows, in Newfoundland, in 1960. He organized its excavation with his wife, Anne Stine Ingstad.

personas/anne-stine-ingstad/resumen.texto: Norwegian archaeologist who directed the excavations at L’Anse aux Meadows between 1961 and 1968 and showed that its buildings and objects, such as a bronze pin and a spindle whorl, were Norse from around the year 1000.

personas/peter-wilhelm-lund/resumen.texto: Danish naturalist who settled in Lagoa Santa (Minas Gerais) and explored hundreds of caves. In the Sumidouro cave he found human bones in 1843, together with remains of extinct fauna, and held that humans had lived alongside those animals, an idea that took almost a century to be accepted.

personas/annette-laming-emperaire/resume.texto: French archaeologist, a specialist in rock art, who directed the French-Brazilian mission in the Lagoa Santa region. In 1974–1975 her team found at the Lapa Vermelha IV rock shelter the skeleton later named Luzia.

personas/george-mcjunkin/resumen.texto: African American cowboy, born enslaved in Texas, who after a flood in 1908 saw large bones in a gully near Folsom (New Mexico). The site, excavated after his death, proved that there were humans in America during the Ice Age.

personas/tom-dillehay/resumen.texto: American archaeologist who has excavated Monte Verde, in southern Chile, since 1977. His monograph and the 1997 visit of a group of specialists led to broad acceptance that there were people in America before Clovis. He also excavated Huaca Prieta, in Peru.

personas/niede-guidon/resumen.texto: Brazilian archaeologist trained in France who has investigated since the 1970s the rock shelters of the Serra da Capivara, in Piauí, and attributed dates of more than 30,000 years to Pedra Furada. She achieved the creation of Serra da Capivara National Park (1979), a World Heritage Site since 1991, and presided over the founding of the Museum of the American Man.

personas/david-meltzer/resumen.texto: American archaeologist specializing in the peopling of the Americas. He was part of the group that in 1997 accepted the antiquity of Monte Verde, criticized with Adovasio and Dillehay the evidence from Pedra Furada (1994) and, with Donald Grayson, the overkill hypothesis (2003).

personas/paul-s-martin/resumen.texto: American paleoecologist who, in the 1960s and in 1973, proposed that newly arrived hunters wiped out the American megafauna within a few centuries (the “overkill” hypothesis). It had followers and critics; the main objection is the scarcity of kill sites.

personas/joseph-greenberg/resumen.texto: American linguist who classified the languages of Africa and who in 1987 proposed grouping almost all the Indigenous languages of America, except the Eskimo-Aleut and Na-Dene, into a single family, “Amerind.” Most specialists in American languages rejected the proposal because of its method.

personas/lyle-campbell/resumen.texto: American linguist specializing in Indigenous languages of America and in historical linguistics. He wrote the most cited critique of Greenberg’s Amerind (1988) and the reference handbook American Indian Languages (1997).

personas/dennis-stanford/resumen.texto: Smithsonian archaeologist who, with Bruce Bradley, proposed the Solutrean hypothesis: that people from western Europe reached America following the edge of the North Atlantic ice during the last glaciation. Most archaeologists and genetic studies reject it.

personas/eske-willerslev/resumen.texto: Danish geneticist who led or coordinated many of the ancient DNA studies on the peopling of the Americas and the Arctic: the Saqqaq Paleo-Eskimo (2010), the Mal’ta child (2014), Anzick-1 (2014), Kennewick Man (2015) and the genomes of 2015 and 2018.

personas/ales-hrdlicka/resumen.texto: Czech-American anthropologist of the Smithsonian Institution. He held that Indigenous Americans arrived from Asia through the Bering Strait area in geologically recent times and rejected all evidence of greater antiquity, including Ameghino’s in Argentina; his authority delayed acceptance of finds such as Folsom.

personas/samuel-hearne/resumen.texto: Explorer for the Hudson’s Bay Company who reached the mouth of the Coppermine River by land in 1771, guided by the Chipewyan Matonabbee. His account, published in 1795, describes the massacre of Inuit at Bloody Falls.

personas/walter-neves/resumen.texto: Brazilian biological anthropologist who named Luzia and argued that the first South Americans had skulls different from those of present-day Indigenous people, which he attributed to an earlier migration from Asia. The ancient genomes studied in 2018 did not show two distinct populations.

personas/junius-bird/resumen.texto: American archaeologist who in 1936–1937 excavated Fell Cave and others in Magallanes and showed that the first hunters at the southern tip of America lived alongside the American horse. He later excavated Huaca Prieta, in Peru, and studied its textiles.

personas/dolores-piperno/resumen.texto: American archaeobotanist of the Smithsonian Institution who, using starch grains and phytoliths, documented maize about 8,700 years old at Xihuatoxtla, in the Balsas Valley, and dated with Kent Flannery the oldest cobs from Guilá Naquitz.

personas/jared-diamond/resumen.texto: American biologist and geographer, author of popular books on global history. In Collapse (2005) he explained the end of the Greenland Norse by their attachment to a European economy and their refusal to learn from the Inuit; specialist archaeologists dispute that explanation.

hechos/poblamiento-de-america/resumen.texto: Ancient and present-day genomes indicate that the ancestors of Indigenous Americans separated from East Asians about 25,000 to 20,000 years ago, spent a time in Beringia and entered the continent in a single great migration, with later contributions in the north (Paleo-Eskimos, Na-Dene, Inuit). Monte Verde, in Chile, shows people at the southern tip about 14,500 years ago; the White Sands footprints suggest presence 23,000 to 21,000 years ago. The date of the first entry and the route (Pacific coast or ice-free corridor) remain under discussion.

hechos/beringia/resumen.texto: During the last glaciation sea level dropped more than a hundred meters and left exposed a strip of land hundreds of kilometers wide between Siberia and Alaska, without large glaciers, which the sea covered again about 11,000 years ago. Geneticists propose that the ancestors of Indigenous Americans were isolated there for several thousand years, where they differentiated from Asians, before expanding southward (the “Beringian standstill”).

hechos/rutas-del-poblamiento-de-america/.texto: Routes of Entry: The Pacific Coast and the Ice-Free Corridor

The classic model assumed that hunters entered through an ice-free corridor between the glaciers of western Canada. Sediment studies show that this corridor could not support hunters until about 12,600 years ago, after the arrival of the first settlers, so many researchers prefer a boat route along the Pacific coast, proposed by Knut Fladmark in 1979. The coastal sites of that time are now under the sea, so that route is hard to prove.

hechos/debate-colonial-sobre-el-origen-d.texto: The Colonial Debate on the Origin of the Indians

In his Natural and Moral History of the Indies (1590), José de Acosta argued that the Indians had arrived little by little, as hunters and more by land than by sea, from some still unknown place, probably in the north, where the Old World joined America or came very close to it, because he did not believe they could have crossed the ocean with their animals. In 1607 Gregorio García gathered the rival theories: the lost tribes of Israel, the Carthaginians, Atlantis and others. Acosta expressly rejected Atlantis and a Hebrew origin; his idea is in essence the one that archaeology and genetics later confirmed, and the others were discarded, although the lost-tribes theory kept circulating.

hechos/hallazgos-de-lund-en-lagoa-santa/.texto: Peter Wilhelm Lund and the Fossil Men of Lagoa Santa

The Danish naturalist Peter Wilhelm Lund explored hundreds of caves in Lagoa Santa (Minas Gerais) and in 1843 found in the Sumidouro cave the remains of several dozen people mixed with the bones of extinct animals. He held that humans had lived alongside that fauna, something the science of his time did not accept and that was confirmed in the 20th century.

hechos/teoria-de-ameghino-sobre-el-orige.texto: Ameghino and the American Origin of Humanity

Florentino Ameghino held that humanity had arisen on the Pampas plain during the Tertiary and had spread from there to the rest of the world, based on remains he attributed to ancient human species. Aleš Hrdlička and other scientists reviewed those remains and sites in 1910 and concluded that they were of recent Indigenous people or of other animals; the theory was discarded. His paleontological work, by contrast, is still valued.

hechos/cultura-folsom/titulo.texto: The Folsom Hunters and the 1927 Evidence

hechos/cultura-folsom/resumen.texto: Hunters of the Great Plains and the Rocky Mountains, successors of Clovis, who hunted an extinct bison with very fine fluted points. In 1927, at the Folsom site (New Mexico), a point was found between the ribs of an extinct bison and seen in situ by several specialists: it was the first accepted evidence of humans in America during the Ice Age, against Hrdlička’s opinion.

hechos/cultura-clovis/resumen.texto: Hunter-gatherer culture defined by its fluted stone points, identified at Blackwater Draw (New Mexico) in the 1930s and spread across almost all of North America. It lasted barely three centuries, between about 13,050 and 12,750 years before the present according to the 2020 dates, and hunted mammoths and mastodons as well as other animals. The genome of the Anzick child (2014) showed that his people belonged to the same population as present-day Indigenous Americans.

hechos/modelo-clovis-primero/titulo.texto: The “Clovis First” Model and Its Fall

hechos/modelo-clovis-primero/resumen.texto: Since the 1960s, most archaeologists held that the Clovis hunters had been the first Americans and rejected every older site proposed, often rightly, for doubtful dates or pieces not clearly human. The model fell in 1997, when a group of specialists, skeptics included, accepted the antiquity of Monte Verde, in Chile.

hechos/aceptacion-de-monte-verde/resumen.texto: In January 1997 a group of archaeologists reviewed Monte Verde and Tom Dillehay’s collections and accepted that the camp was about 14,500 calibrated years old, more than a millennium before Clovis. The site, preserved under peat, has remains of wooden houses, medicinal plants, seaweed brought from the coast and bones of gomphotheres, a relative of the mastodon. Stuart Fiedel and others later criticized the documentation of the pieces; Dillehay responded and most maintained their acceptance.

hechos/huellas-de-white-sands/titulo.texto: The Human Footprints of White Sands

hechos/huellas-de-white-sands/resumen.texto: On the shore of an ancient lake in New Mexico, hundreds of human footprints are preserved, mostly of children and adolescents, together with those of mammoths and giant ground sloths. In 2021 they were dated, using seeds of an aquatic plant, to about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago; critics such as David Madsen objected that these seeds can yield ages that are too old, and in 2023 pollen and quartz grains from the same layers gave matching ages. If they are accepted, they show that people lived south of the ice sheets during the full glaciation.

hechos/debate-de-pedra-furada/resumen.texto: Niède Guidon published in 1986 dates of up to about 32,000 years for charcoal and worked stones from the Pedra Furada rock shelter, in Piauí. After visiting the site, David Meltzer, James Adovasio and Tom Dillehay argued in 1994 that the stones could have broken when they fell from the cliff and that the fires could have been natural. Guidon’s team, and later Eric Boëda (2014), defended the ancient occupation; the question remains open.

hechos/luzia/titulo.texto: Luzia, one of the oldest skeletons in the Americas

hechos/luzia/resumen.texto: Skeleton of a young woman about 11,500 years old, found in 1974–1975 in the Lapa Vermelha IV rock shelter, in the Lagoa Santa region, by the mission led by Annette Laming-Emperaire. Walter Neves, who named her, interpreted her skull as resembling those of Australia and Melanesia and proposed an early, distinct migration; ancient genomes from the region (2018) showed that the people of Lagoa Santa descended from the same population as other Indigenous Americans. Her skull was damaged in the fire at the National Museum of Rio de Janeiro in 2018 and was partly rescued.

hechos/debate-de-la-senal-australasiana/.texto: In 2015 a team found, in Amazonian peoples such as the Suruí and the Karitiana, a small genetic component related to populations of Australasia, which it attributed to an unknown founding population (“Y population”); another team, led by Raghavan, explained it as a minor, later admixture. In 2018 traces of that signal appeared in a genome from Lagoa Santa about 10,400 years old (Moreno-Mayar et al.), but not in the other ancient genomes studied that year (Posth et al.); how it reached South America remains unclear.

hechos/nino-de-malta/titulo.texto: The Mal’ta Boy and the Dual Ancestry of Indigenous Americans

hechos/nino-de-malta/resumen.texto: A boy buried about 24,000 years ago at Mal’ta, near Lake Baikal, belonged to a population of northern Eurasia related both to Western Europeans and to Indigenous Americans. His genome (2014) showed that part of the American ancestry comes from that population and the rest from a population of East Asia.

hechos/entierro-de-anzick/resumen.texto: A child of one or two years was buried in Montana about 12,600 years ago with more than a hundred Clovis-style stone and bone tools, covered in red ochre; it is the only known Clovis burial. His genome (2014) showed that he belonged to the population from which many living Indigenous peoples descend. In 2014 his remains were reburied in a ceremony attended by representatives of several tribes.

hechos/ninos-de-upward-sun-river/titulo.texto: The Upward Sun River Children and the Ancient Beringians

hechos/ninos-de-upward-sun-river/resumen.texto: At a campsite in Alaska, the cremated remains of a child of about three years were found and, beneath them, the burial of two infants with grave goods, about 11,500 years old. The genome of one of the infants defined a branch of the first Americans, the “Ancient Beringians,” which split off from the others about 20,000 years ago and left no known descendants.

hechos/disputa-por-el-hombre-de-kennewic.texto: In 1996 the remains of a man about 8,500 years old were found on the banks of the Columbia River, with a stone point lodged in his hip and bone healed around it. Several tribes claimed them for burial under the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA, 1990); a group of scientists sued for the right to study them and won in 2002 and in 2004, because no link to present-day peoples had been proven. His genome (2015) showed that link, above all with the Confederated Tribes of the Colville, and in 2017 the remains were buried in an undisclosed place.

hechos/mastodonte-de-cerutti/titulo.texto: The Cerutti Mastodon: A 130,000-Year Age Rejected by Most

hechos/mastodonte-de-cerutti/resumen.texto: In 2017 a team interpreted broken mastodon bones and stones found beside them in San Diego, dated to about 130,000 years ago, as the work of unknown hominins. Most archaeologists reject that interpretation: there are no shaped tools, and the fractures may be due to the machinery that exposed the site or to other natural causes.

hechos/cueva-del-chiquihuite/titulo.texto: Chiquihuite Cave: Disputed Tools About 30,000 Years Old

hechos/cueva-del-chiquihuite/resumen.texto: In 2020 Ciprian Ardelean and his team presented nearly two thousand stones from a high-altitude cave in Zacatecas, in layers dated to about 30,000 years ago, as human tools. Several specialists maintain that they are stones broken by natural causes; the site has no human remains and no clear hearths.

hechos/extincion-de-la-megafauna-america.texto: At the end of the last glaciation, about 35 genera of large mammals disappeared from North America and more than 50 from South America: mammoths, mastodons, horses, camels, giant ground sloths, glyptodonts and others. Paul Martin (1973) attributed this to hunting by the newcomers (“overkill”); Donald Grayson and David Meltzer (2003) note that there are only about fourteen North American sites with proven hunting, all of mammoth or mastodon, and give more weight to climate change. Many researchers today accept a combination of climate and hunting, with different weight depending on the region.

hechos/hipotesis-del-impacto-del-dryas-r.texto: In 2007 a group of researchers proposed that a comet fell or exploded over North America about 12,900 years ago, causing fires, the cooling of the Younger Dryas, the extinction of megafauna and the end of the Clovis culture. Other teams failed to replicate their indicators or found terrestrial explanations for them, and in 2023 a review declared the hypothesis refuted; its defenders continue to maintain it.

hechos/hipotesis-solutrense/resumen.texto: Dennis Stanford and Bruce Bradley proposed from 1999 that the ancestors of the Clovis people arrived from France and the Iberian Peninsula, following the edge of the ice in the North Atlantic. Critics pointed out that the Solutrean ended about five thousand years before Clovis and that there is no evidence for such a voyage, and the genome of Anzick-1 (2014) showed that the Clovis people were of Asian and American ancestry, with no European contribution. Racist groups used the hypothesis to deny that Indigenous peoples were the first Americans, something its authors did not maintain.

hechos/clasificacion-amerindia-de-greenb.texto: In 1987 Joseph Greenberg proposed that almost all the Indigenous languages of the Americas, except the Eskimo-Aleut and Na-Dene languages, formed a single family, Amerind, and linked it to one of three migrations. Lyle Campbell and most specialists rejected it, because its method of comparing word lists does not distinguish kinship from chance or borrowing. Today more than a hundred families and isolated languages without demonstrated kinship are recognized in the Americas.

hechos/domesticacion-del-maiz/resumen.texto: Maize descends from teosinte of the Balsas River valley, in southwestern Mexico, which genetics indicates was domesticated only once, about 9,000 years ago (Matsuoka et al., 2002). The oldest remains are starch grains and phytoliths about 8,700 years old from the Xihuatoxtla rock shelter (Piperno, 2009), and the oldest directly dated cobs, about 6,250 years old, come from Guilá Naquitz (Oaxaca). From there it spread to the Andes and eastern North America and became the basis of the continent’s farming societies.

hechos/domesticacion-de-la-papa/resumen.texto: According to genetic studies, the potato was domesticated only once, on the highlands of southern Peru, north of Lake Titicaca, from wild potatoes, between about 10,000 and 7,000 years ago. Andean peoples developed thousands of varieties and preservation techniques such as chuño, freeze-dried and dehydrated potato. Taken to Europe in the 16th century, it became a staple food of the world.

hechos/domesticacion-de-la-mandioca/resu.texto: Cassava was domesticated on the southern edge of the Amazon basin, in present-day Brazil, from a wild subspecies of the same plant, according to genetics (Olsen and Schaal, 1999); the date is estimated at about 8,000 to 10,000 years ago, with no remains that old to confirm it. Its roots contain toxic compounds, and Amazonian peoples developed techniques to remove them, such as grating and pressing.

hechos/domesticacion-del-zapallo/resumen.texto: Seeds and rinds of Cucurbita pepo from the Guilá Naquitz cave (Oaxaca), directly dated, show traits of domestication from between about 10,000 and 8,000 years ago (Smith, 1997). Squash and the bottle gourd, used as a container, are among the first cultivated plants of the Americas, thousands of years before maize.

hechos/domesticacion-del-frijol/titulo.texto: The Domestication of the Common Bean

hechos/domesticacion-del-frijol/resumen.texto: Genetic studies indicate that the common bean was domesticated separately in Mesoamerica and in the Andes. Beans from the Guitarrero cave (Peru), which had been attributed to about 10,000 years, turned out to be about 4,300 radiocarbon years old when dated directly (Kaplan and Lynch, 1999), and direct dates from Mexico do not exceed that antiquity either, although domestication may be earlier. Together with maize and squash, it formed the base of the Mesoamerican agricultural diet.

hechos/domesticacion-de-la-quinua/resume.texto: The peoples of the Lake Titicaca basin gathered and cultivated Chenopodium species for millennia. At Chiripa (Bolivia), beside the lake, domesticated forms of quinoa with thin-coated seeds were already being cultivated around 1500 BC (Bruno and Whitehead, 2003). Together with the potato, it was one of the staple foods of the highlands.

hechos/domesticacion-de-la-llama-y-la-al.texto: The Domestication of the Llama, the Alpaca and the Guinea Pig

On the Junín puna (Peru), sites such as Telarmachay show the shift from hunting wild camelids to raising them about 6,000 to 5,500 years ago, according to the studies of Jane Wheeler. Genetics confirmed that the llama descends from the guanaco and the alpaca from the vicuña. Llamas and alpacas provided pack transport, wool, meat and dung to Andean societies, which also domesticated the guinea pig (cuy), at a less precisely known date.

hechos/domesticacion-del-pavo/resumen.texto: The oldest turkeys raised outside their natural range appear at El Mirador (Guatemala), brought from central Mexico between 300 BC and AD 100. In the southwestern United States a distinct lineage was raised, mainly for its feathers, according to ancient DNA; the turkey and the dog were the main domestic animals of Mesoamerica. The Spanish took it to Europe in the 16th century.

hechos/contacto-entre-polinesios-y-ameri.texto: Contact Between Polynesians and Indigenous Americans

The genomes of several islands of eastern Polynesia, from the Marquesas to Rapa Nui, carry a small Indigenous American ancestry related to the Zenú of Colombia, incorporated around 1150–1230 according to the 2020 study. Together with the sweet potato, an American crop that the Polynesians had before the Europeans, it shows contact before Columbus, although it is not known whether the Polynesians or the Americans did the travelling.

hechos/paleoesquimales/resumen.texto: About 4,500 to 5,000 years ago a population of hunters arrived from Siberia and spread rapidly from Alaska to Greenland with very small stone tools, the “Arctic Small Tool tradition.” Its regional cultures (Independence, Saqqaq, Pre-Dorset and later Dorset) were, according to genetics, a single population, distinct from both Indigenous Americans and the Inuit.

hechos/cultura-saqqaq/resumen.texto: The first known culture of southern and western Greenland, of hunters of seals, caribou and birds. In 2010 the genome of a Saqqaq man was sequenced from a lock of hair about 4,000 years old preserved in the ice at Qeqertasussuk: it was the first complete genome of an ancient human and showed his origin in northeastern Siberia.

hechos/cultura-dorset/resumen.texto: A Paleo-Eskimo culture of the eastern Arctic, from Newfoundland to Greenland, with semi-subterranean houses and an art of small carvings in ivory, bone and wood; it did not use the bow or draft dogs. It disappeared around 1300–1500, shortly after the arrival of the Thule, with almost no mixing with them. Inuit oral tradition remembers the “Tuniit,” a strong and elusive people who had lived in those lands before, and some accounts speak of struggles with them.

hechos/cultura-thule/resumen.texto: The culture of the ancestors of the Inuit, which emerged in northern Alaska and from the 13th century spread rapidly to Greenland with draft dogs, sledges, kayaks, large skin boats (umiak) and harpoons for hunting whales. Soon after their arrival the Dorset disappeared, and they reached Greenland while the Norse were living there: Norse objects (iron, chain mail, pieces of cloth) have been found at their sites. The name comes from the Thule region, in northwestern Greenland.

hechos/pueblo-inuit/resumen.texto: Arctic peoples of Canada, Greenland and northern Alaska (where they are called Iñupiat), descendants of the Thule and speakers of closely related languages. They lived by hunting seals, walruses, whales and caribou, in family groups with leaders who had no formal power, shamans (angakkut) and rules for sharing the catch. There were wars between groups and with their Indian neighbors, blood vengeance and infanticide in times of famine, documented by oral tradition and by the first European observers.

hechos/pueblos-yupik/resumen.texto: Peoples of western and southwestern Alaska and the far northeast of Siberia, related to the Inuit in language and origin. The Alaskan Yupik lived in villages with a communal men’s house, hunted marine mammals and fished for salmon; their oral tradition remembers the “bow and arrow wars” between villages, which predate the arrival of the Russians.

hechos/pueblo-aleutiano/resumen.texto: A people of the Aleutian Islands and the Alaska Peninsula, inhabited for about 9,000 years. Hunters of marine mammals from kayaks, they had a society divided into nobles, commoners and slaves taken in war. From 1745 Russian fur hunters subjugated them with violence and forced labor, and war and epidemics greatly reduced their population.

hechos/guerras-entre-los-pueblos-del-art.texto: The Wars Among the Peoples of Northwest Alaska

According to the oral tradition gathered by the anthropologist Ernest Burch, the Iñupiat nations of northwestern Alaska fought wars among themselves and with the Yupik and the Athabaskans until the mid-19th century, with surprise raids at dawn, massacres of entire villages and armor of bone and ivory plates. These wars coexisted with alliances, trade fairs and marriages between groups.

hechos/matanza-de-bloody-falls/resumen.texto: On July 17, 1771, near the mouth of the Coppermine River, the Chipewyan and other Dene accompanying Samuel Hearne, guided by Matonabbee, attacked a camp of Copper Inuit at dawn and killed about twenty people, among them women. Hearne witnessed it and recounted it in his 1795 book, published after his death with additions by the editor. It is the best-documented episode of the enmity between the Dene and the Inuit, which the place remembers in its name.

hechos/quinta-expedicion-de-thule/resume.texto: A Danish expedition led by Knud Rasmussen that studied the Inuit of the central Canadian Arctic and then crossed by sledge to Alaska. It gathered oral tradition, objects and measurements, showed that the Inuit from Greenland to Alaska spoke variants of a single language and, with the excavations of Therkel Mathiassen, defined the Thule culture.

hechos/erik-el-rojo-coloniza-groenlandia.texto: Erik the Red Takes Settlers to Greenland

According to the Book of the Icelanders, fourteen or fifteen years before Iceland adopted Christianity, Erik the Red, banished for homicide, took settlers to the island he had explored and named Greenland. The Book of Settlements says that of twenty-five ships, fourteen arrived. The settlers found remains of dwellings, skin boats and stone tools of an earlier people, which they associated with the skrælingar of Vinland.

hechos/colonias-nordicas-de-groenlandia/.texto: For almost five centuries the Norse occupied two areas of southwestern Greenland, the Eastern Settlement and the Western Settlement, with hundreds of farms and a population of a few thousand people (the most cited estimates range from 2,000 to 3,000). They lived from livestock, hunting seals and caribou, and selling to Europe ivory and hides of walruses hunted in the north; they had their own bishopric from 1124 and submitted to the king of Norway in 1261. The Western Settlement was abandoned around the mid-14th century and the Eastern in the 15th century.

hechos/nordicos-en-vinlandia-segun-las-s.texto: The Norse in Vinland According to the Sagas: Trade and Violence

The two Vinland sagas recount several expeditions from Greenland around the year 1000. They tell that the men of Thorvald Eriksson killed eight sleeping natives and that he died in the attack that followed; that Karlsefni traded with the skrælingar and then fought with them and, according to the Saga of Erik the Red, took two native children from Markland, whom he baptized and taught his language; and that Freydís had her Icelandic partners killed. The sagas were written two centuries later and do not agree with each other; the location of their places, apart from L'Anse aux Meadows as a possible base, is disputed.

hechos/descubrimiento-de-l-anse-aux-mead.texto: The Discovery of L'Anse aux Meadows

In 1960 Helge Ingstad, guided by the neighbor George Decker, identified in northern Newfoundland some mounds that turned out to be ruins of turf buildings. Excavations by Anne Stine Ingstad between 1961 and 1968 found Norse objects and dates from around the year 1000: it was the first archaeological evidence that the Norse reached America, as the sagas said, although it does not confirm every place or every episode of their accounts.

hechos/nordicos-en-l-anse-aux-meadows-en.texto: The Norse Felled Trees at L'Anse aux Meadows in 1021

Three pieces of wood cut with metal tools at L'Anse aux Meadows preserve in their rings the mark of a cosmic radiation spike of the year 993. By counting the rings that followed, a 2021 study dated the felling to 1021: it is the first exact year of European presence in the Americas.

hechos/groenlandia-se-somete-a-noruega/t.texto: Greenland Submits to the King of Norway

hechos/groenlandia-se-somete-a-noruega/r.texto: According to the Icelandic annals and the saga of King Haakon IV, in 1261 the Greenlanders agreed to pay tribute to the king of Norway, one year before the Icelanders. Trade with the island thereafter fell into the hands of the Norwegian crown and of ships based in Bergen, and voyages became increasingly rare.

hechos/abandono-del-asentamiento-occiden.texto: The Abandonment of the Western Settlement

According to the account attributed to Ívar Bárðarson, when he went to the Western Settlement around the mid-14th century, he found it without people and with livestock running loose, and attributed this to the skrælingar. Excavations, such as that of the “farm under the sand,” show an abandonment during those decades, with no clear signs of attack; cooling, isolation or emigration have been proposed.

hechos/ataque-de-los-skraelingar-de-1379.texto: The Icelandic annals record that in 1379 the skrælingar attacked the Greenlanders, killed eighteen men and took two boys as slaves. It is the only armed clash between Norse and Inuit recorded in the Norse writings of Greenland; the Inuit oral tradition collected by Hinrich Rink in the 19th century also remembers struggles with the Norse, in which people died on both sides.

hechos/boda-de-hvalsey/titulo.texto: The Hvalsey Wedding, the Last Record of the Norse of Greenland

hechos/boda-de-hvalsey/resumen.texto: In September 1408 Sigríður Björnsdóttir and Þorsteinn Ólafsson, Icelanders who had arrived on a ship blown off course, were married in the church at Hvalsey. A letter from Greenlandic priests and later testimony from Icelanders, preserved in Iceland, attest to it, and the annals record that a year earlier a man accused of seducing a married woman with witchcraft was burned in Greenland. These are the last written reports of the colony.

hechos/desaparicion-de-los-nordicos-de-g.texto: The Disappearance of the Norse of Greenland

After 1408 there are no more written reports of the colony, and archaeology indicates that the Eastern Settlement was emptied around the mid-15th century. Proposed causes include the cooling of the Little Ice Age, the fall in the price of walrus ivory against elephant ivory, the end of trade with Norway, gradual emigration to Iceland and conflicts with the Inuit. Jared Diamond (2005) attributed the end to the rigidity of their economy and their contempt for the Inuit; specialists object that isotopes show an increasingly marine diet and prefer economic and demographic causes.

hechos/mapa-de-vinlandia/resumen.texto: A world map that appeared in 1957, attributed to the 15th century, showing Vinland to the west of Greenland; Yale University presented it in 1965 as the first map of America. Since 1974 analyses have found titanium dioxide in its ink in the anatase form, a pigment of the 20th century, and in 2021 Yale announced that it was a forgery. It proves nothing about Norse voyages, which are known from the sagas and archaeology.

hechos/piedra-runica-de-kensington/resum.texto: A stone slab with runes that the Swedish immigrant Olof Öhman said he found in 1898 in his field in Minnesota, recounting a Norse voyage in 1362. In 1910 the geologist Newton Winchell believed it was old, but the linguist George Flom concluded that its runes and language were not those of the 14th century; since then most specialists have considered it a 19th-century forgery. It still has defenders outside academia.

hechos/viajes-de-frobisher/titulo.texto: Frobisher’s Voyages and the Captured Inuit

hechos/viajes-de-frobisher/resumen.texto: Martin Frobisher made three voyages to Baffin Island in search of the Northwest Passage and gold. In 1576 five of his sailors disappeared ashore after dealing with the Inuit, and Frobisher captured an Inuk to exchange him; in 1577 he took a man, a woman and their son. The four captives died in England shortly afterward, and in 1577 his men killed several Inuit in a fight. The Inuit oral tradition recorded by Charles Francis Hall in 1861 still remembered the five sailors, who according to it lived for a time among the Inuit.

hechos/expediciones-danesas-a-groenlandi.texto: King Christian IV of Denmark sent three expeditions to search for the Norse of Greenland and assert sovereignty. They found none of them, traded and clashed with the Inuit, and forcibly took several of them to Denmark.
