In 1612, on an English voyage, an Inuk killed James Hall, the pilot of those expeditions, with a spear, according to accounts of that voyage, in revenge for the abductions of 1605.

hechos/llegada-de-hans-egede/resumen.texto: In July 1721 the pastor Hans Egede landed with his wife, his four children and about forty colonists near present-day Nuuk, with the support of the king of Denmark and Norway and of a company from Bergen, to find the Norse again and bring them the Reformation. He found only Inuit and devoted himself to preaching Christianity to them and learning their language; his arrival is taken as the beginning of Danish colonization of Greenland.

hechos/fundacion-de-godthab/resumen.texto: In 1728 Governor Claus Paarss moved Egede’s mission and post to the mainland and founded Godthåb. The expedition, with soldiers and convicts, suffered scurvy and mutinies; many died, and in 1731 the crown withdrew almost everyone. Egede stayed with his family. Godthåb survived as the seat of the mission and of trade and is the present capital, Nuuk.

hechos/epidemia-de-viruela-de-1733/resum.texto: Smallpox arrived in 1733 on the mission ship, with a young Greenlander returning from Copenhagen, and spread along the west-central coast, where the Inuit had no defenses against it. A large part of the population of the area died; estimates range from about 2,000 to more than 3,000 people. Hans Egede, his wife Gertrud Rask and the Moravian missionaries attended the sick, and many survivors came to the missions afterward.

hechos/mision-morava-en-groenlandia/resu.texto: In 1733 the Moravian brothers Christian David and the cousins Matthäus and Christian Stach arrived at Godthåb, sent from Herrnhut by Count Zinzendorf, and founded the mission of Neu-Herrnhut. They rivaled Egede’s Lutheran mission, baptized their first convert in 1739 and later opened other stations in the south; in 1900 they handed their congregations over to the Danish church.

hechos/monopolio-comercial-danes-en-groe.texto: The Danish Trade Monopoly in Greenland

In 1774 the Danish state created the Royal Greenland Trade, which held the monopoly on the island’s trade and administered it until 1908, with Greenland closed to foreign ships. It bought seal and whale oil and furs at fixed prices and sold European goods; the closure limited contact with other Europeans, and the trade monopoly lasted until 1950.

hechos/extincion-de-los-sadlermiut/resum.texto: The Sadlermiut, a small Inuit group that lived almost in isolation on Southampton Island and other islands of Hudson Bay, nearly all died in the winter of 1902–1903 from a contagious disease, perhaps typhus, typhoid fever or influenza, attributed to a sick sailor from the Scottish whaler Active: of 58 people, one woman and four children survived. Because of their distinct culture they were considered the last Dorset, but genetic studies showed them to be descendants of the Thule, without Dorset admixture.

hechos/atuagagdliutit/titulo.texto: Atuagagdliutit, the First Newspaper in Greenlandic

hechos/atuagagdliutit/resumen.texto: In 1861 Hinrich Rink founded in Godthåb Atuagagdliutit (“What Is Offered to Read”), an illustrated newspaper in Greenlandic printed at the local press. It published world news, Inuit stories and legends, with engravings by Aron of Kangeq and other Greenlanders, and it still appears, merged with the Danish newspaper Grønlandsposten.

hechos/mision-morava-de-labrador/resumen.texto: In 1771 Moravian missionaries, who had learned Greenlandic in the missions of Greenland and could therefore speak with the Inuit of Labrador, founded Nain on the Labrador coast, with permission from the British government. It was the first of several coastal stations, where they preached, traded and taught reading and writing in Inuktitut.

hechos/inuit-de-labrador-en-la-muestra-d.texto: The Labrador Inuit in Hagenbeck’s Exhibitions

In 1880 Abraham Ulrikab, an Inuk from the Moravian mission of Hebron, his family and four other Labrador Inuit, eight people in all, agreed to be exhibited in the ethnographic shows organized by Carl Hagenbeck, owner of the Hamburg zoo. They were not vaccinated against smallpox in time, and all died in Germany and France between late 1880 and January 1881. The diary that Abraham wrote in Inuktitut survived in a German translation made by the missionaries.

hechos/inughuit-llevados-a-nueva-york/ti.texto: The Inughuit Peary Took to New York

hechos/inughuit-llevados-a-nueva-york/re.texto: In 1897 the explorer Robert Peary brought six Inughuit (Inuit of the far northwest of Greenland) from Greenland to New York. They were placed in the care of the American Museum of Natural History and studied by its staff. The adults and one child soon died of tuberculosis; the museum deceived Minik, a boy, with a mock burial of his father, Qisuk, whose skeleton it displayed. The case became an example of the treatment of Indigenous people as objects of study.

lugares/l-anse-aux-meadows/resumen.texto: The only confirmed Norse settlement in the Americas, at the northern tip of Newfoundland: eight turf buildings with wooden frames, a smithy and boat-repair workshops, occupied briefly. Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad identified it in 1960 and excavated it between 1961 and 1968; in 2021 tree rings from wood cut with metal tools gave the year 1021. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1978.

lugares/brattahlid/resumen.texto: Farm of Erik the Red in Erik’s Fjord, today Qassiarsuk, center of the Eastern Settlement of the Norse of Greenland. Ruins of houses, barns and a small turf church with its cemetery survive; the church was found in 1961 and is associated by tradition with Thjodhild, Erik’s wife.

lugares/gardar/resumen.texto: Seat of the bishopric of Greenland, today Igaliku, created around 1124 at the request of the Greenlanders; its first bishop, Arnaldo, arrived in 1126. It was the first Catholic bishopric in the Americas and had a stone cathedral dedicated to Saint Nicholas; from the late 14th century the bishops who were appointed no longer traveled to the island.

lugares/hvalsey/resumen.texto: The best-preserved stone church of Norse Greenland, in the Eastern Settlement. A wedding recorded in Icelandic letters was held there in 1408, the last documented event of the colony.

lugares/herjolfsnes/resumen.texto: Farm and harbor at the southern tip of the Eastern Settlement, where the ships arriving from Norway and Iceland put in. In its cemetery, Poul Nørlund excavated in 1921 woolen clothing from the last years of the colony, preserved by the frozen ground, with cuts similar to the European fashion of the time.

lugares/nuuk/resumen.texto: Capital of Greenland. It grew out of the mission and trading post that Hans Egede founded in 1721 on a nearby island, which Governor Claus Paarss moved in 1728 to the mainland under the name Godthåb (“good hope”). The Moravian mission of Neu-Herrnhut (1733) was also established there and, in the 19th century, the printing press and the first newspaper in Greenlandic.

lugares/blackwater-draw/resumen.texto: Former lake near Clovis (New Mexico) where, from 1929 and in the excavations of 1932–1937, fluted points appeared together with mammoth bones. It is the type site of the Clovis culture and also preserves Folsom layers and those of later periods.

lugares/folsom-site/resumen.texto: Gully in northeastern New Mexico where, between 1926 and 1928, stone fluted points appeared among the skeletons of about thirty bison of an extinct species. It was the first accepted proof that humans were in the Americas during the Ice Age.

lugares/upward-sun-river/resumen.texto: Camp in the Tanana Valley, Alaska, with the cremated remains of a child (found in 2010) and the burial of two infants (2013), about 11,500 years old. The genome of one of the infants defined the “Ancient Beringians,” a branch of the first Americans that left no known descendants.

lugares/bluefish-caves/resumen.texto: Three small caves in northern Yukon, excavated by Jacques Cinq-Mars between 1977 and 1987. A new date on bones with cut marks (Bourgeon et al., 2017) gave about 24,000 calibrated years, which would make them the oldest site in North America, but some archaeologists doubt that the marks are human.

lugares/paisley-caves/resumen.texto: Caves in the Oregon desert where human coprolites were found, with DNA of Indigenous American lineages dated to about 14,300 calibrated years ago (Gilbert et al., 2008), earlier than Clovis. The possible contamination of the DNA was debated; later work confirmed points of the Western Stemmed tradition from the same period.

lugares/meadowcroft/resumen.texto: Rock shelter in Pennsylvania, excavated since 1973 by James Adovasio, with a sequence of occupations spanning thousands of years. Its deepest layers gave dates of about 16,000 radiocarbon years, which critics attributed to contamination by mineral coal; Adovasio denied this, and today many accept it as a pre-Clovis site.

lugares/pedra-furada/resumen.texto: Large rock shelter in Serra da Capivara National Park (Piauí, Brazil), with cave paintings and a long occupation sequence. Niède Guidon attributed more than 30,000 years to its deepest layers; the Holocene occupation is not disputed, but the Pleistocene occupation remains under debate.

lugares/lapa-do-santo/resumen.texto: Rock shelter in the Lagoa Santa region (Minas Gerais) with dozens of burials about 10,000 to 8,000 years old, some with ritual manipulation of the bodies (defleshing, separated skulls). Some of the South American genomes studied in 2018, among the oldest, came from its skeletons.

lugares/taima-taima/resumen.texto: Spring in Falcón state (Venezuela) where José María Cruxent, and later Ruth Gruhn and Alan Bryan, found a young mastodon with a fragment of an El Jobo-type point in its pelvis. Its dates of about 13,000 to 14,000 radiocarbon years would make it earlier than Clovis, but both the association and the dates have been disputed.

lugares/cueva-fell/resumen.texto: Cave in southern Chilean Patagonia, near the Strait of Magellan, excavated by Junius Bird in 1936–1937. Its lower layers, about 11,000 radiocarbon years old, contain “fishtail” points with bones of American horse and guanaco: it is one of the key sites of the first South American hunters.

lugares/guila-naquitz/resumen.texto: Small cave in the Oaxaca Valley, excavated by Kent Flannery in 1966. It holds squash seeds (Cucurbita pepo) from domesticated plants about 10,000 to 8,000 years old and the oldest directly dated maize cobs, about 6,250 years old.

lugares/coxcatlan/resumen.texto: Cave in the Tehuacán Valley (Puebla) excavated by Richard MacNeish in the 1960s, with a long sequence of foragers and early farmers. Its small cobs were considered the oldest in the Americas until direct dating in the 1980s showed them to be more recent than had been calculated.

lugares/huaca-prieta/resumen.texto: Mound on the north coast of Peru, in the Chicama Valley, excavated by Junius Bird in 1946–1947 and by Tom Dillehay since 2007. According to Dillehay, its occupation begins around 14,500 years ago; it has very old cotton textiles, one of them dyed with indigo about 6,000 years ago, and early remains of squash, beans, avocado and bottle gourd.

lugares/guitarrero/resumen.texto: Cave in the Callejón de Huaylas (Áncash, Peru), excavated by Thomas Lynch since 1968. It holds cords and textile fragments about 12,000 years old, among the oldest in South America, and domesticated beans whose age was lowered when they were dated directly.

lugares/ipiutak/resumen.texto: Large settlement at Point Hope, in northwestern Alaska, excavated by Helge Larsen, Froelich Rainey and Louis Giddings from 1939: hundreds of houses and graves with very elaborate ivory carvings. It belongs to the late Paleo-Eskimo Ipiutak culture, of the first centuries AD.

lugares/qilakitsoq/resumen.texto: Site on the northwest coast of Greenland where, in 1972, eight Inuit bodies mummified by the cold were found: six women and two children buried around 1475 in their fur clothing. They are a unique source on the clothing, health and life of the Inuit of the period.

lugares/port-au-choix/resumen.texto: Site in northwestern Newfoundland with a Maritime Archaic cemetery about 4,000 years old, excavated since the late 1960s, and a large Dorset village, Phillip’s Garden, from the first centuries AD. It shows the succession of seal-hunting peoples on the Atlantic coast before the Inuit and the Norse.

lugares/kodlunarn-island/resumen.texto: Islet in Frobisher Bay where Martin Frobisher’s men dug trenches in 1577 and 1578 to extract an ore they believed contained gold; traces of those works survive. Its Inuit name means “island of the white people,” and oral tradition remembered those visitors almost three centuries later.

lugares/skraeling-island/resumen.texto: Islet off the east coast of Ellesmere Island, in the Canadian Arctic, where Peter Schledermann excavated 13th-century Thule houses with objects of Norse origin, such as fragments of chain mail and boat rivets. It is one of the pieces of evidence of contact between the Thule and the Norse of Greenland.

lugares/arroyo-seco-2/resumen.texto: Site on the Pampas plain, near Tres Arroyos (Buenos Aires province), with megafauna bones such as American horse and giant ground sloth, together with stone tools, dated to about 14,000 calibrated years according to Gustavo Politis and his team (2016); some researchers dispute the association. It also has a Holocene hunter-gatherer cemetery with dozens of burials.
